rows.w: Reading Terminal Market's roast-pork counter — #1 on Philadelphia Magazine's roast-pork list and The Infatuation's pick for the best sandwich in the market.
Rittenhouse boutique steakhouse — LaBan's gold standard for dry-aged rib-eye and home of the famous luxury cheesesteak; Infatuation 'city's best steakhouse'; Philly Mag Best of Philly.
Jim's (founded 1939 in West Philly) opened its Art Deco South Street shop on July 5, 1976 — the line on 4th and South is a South Street landmark.
Matt Cahn's Washington Square West sandwich shop (with a Fishtown sibling) that rose fast into the city's best-hoagie ranks.
Old City family deli (Inquirer 20 best hoagies; Philly Mag hoagie guide).
Old City's late-night cheesesteak counter — 'what Pat's and Geno's are to South Philly' (Visit Philly late-night guide; Infatuation Old City guide). HELD lead cleared.

Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025, inaugural Philadelphia selection) — strong food at good value. Michelin singled out its 'serious, hefty cheesesteaks bound with Cooper Sharp cheese or long hot whiz'; third in the Inquirer's 2023 best-cheesesteak bracket.

The South Philly shack (open since the 1930s) that Craig LaBan named the city's best cheesesteak in 2002 and that finished second in the Inquirer's 2023 bracket; its juicy roast pork with sautéed spinach earned a James Beard America's Classics award.

Where the cheesesteak began: hot-dog vendor Pat Olivieri started selling thin-sliced steak on a roll here in the 1930s (cheese came in the '40s). Measured honestly: it is the historic origin and a 24-hour 9th-and-Passyunk spectacle rather than critics' best steak — go for the history, go to Angelo's/Dalessandro's/John's for the sandwich.
A fifth-generation Italian deli in South Philly building hoagies of coteghino, mortadella, soppressata, capicola and prosciutto on Sarcone's rolls.
Queen Village deli at the top of recent best-hoagie rankings, with a dozen cold hoagies on Cacia's rolls.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025, inaugural Philadelphia selection) — strong food at good value. Queen Village's century-plus Jewish deli on Fourth Street.

rows.w: Tom Peters' 1997 Belgian beer bar — 'a church where beer nerds worship'; Peters has three James Beard nominations; LaBan, Infatuation.
Where the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the Constitution (1787) were debated and signed — a UNESCO World Heritage Site run by the National Park Service; free timed tickets.
Built 1727–44, the Anglican church where George Washington, Benjamin Franklin and Betsy Ross worshipped; its steeple was once the tallest structure in the colonies.
America's great public market, under a former railroad trainshed since 1893: roast pork, Amish counters, Bassetts ice cream and 70-plus merchants.
Reading Terminal Market's roast-pork counter — #1 on Philadelphia Magazine's roast-pork list and The Infatuation's pick for the best sandwich in the market.

One MICHELIN Star in the inaugural 2025 Michelin Guide Northeast Cities (Philadelphia) selection. Also the 2023 James Beard Outstanding Restaurant winner; its upstairs Lover's Bar was a 2025 JBF Outstanding Bar semifinalist.
Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Indian), Inquirer 'The 76' and LaBan favourite, Infatuation review — a heartfelt tribute to South Indian home cooking.

A 158-year-old Old City candy storefront, restored in 2011 by the Franklin Fountain's Berley brothers — Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Chocolate), Inquirer, Visit Philly (Time Out's #3 US candy store).
Stephen Starr's art-deco steakhouse, the Center City power-meal room — Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Steakhouse, Best Burger), Infatuation, Inquirer best steakhouses.
Rittenhouse boutique steakhouse — LaBan's gold standard for dry-aged rib-eye and home of the famous luxury cheesesteak; Infatuation 'city's best steakhouse'; Philly Mag Best of Philly.
The 2,080-lb cracked bell, an abolitionist-adopted icon of liberty, displayed in an NPS pavilion facing Independence Hall; free.
Franklin Court: Robert Venturi's steel 'ghost structures' outlining Franklin's lost house, the underground Benjamin Franklin Museum and a working 18th-century printing office.

Continuously inhabited since 1720 — one of America's oldest residential streets: 32 craftsmen's houses, two of them a small museum.
Steps from Independence Hall, it traces the colonies from unrest to independence; centrepiece is George Washington's original headquarters tent.
The world's only museum dedicated to the US Constitution, with Signers' Hall's 42 life-size bronze framers.
Opened 1829 as the world's first true 'penitentiary' (solitary reform), closed 1971, now a crumbling, haunting museum — Al Capone's cell is furnished.
Philadelphia's hands-on science museum — walk-through Giant Heart, Baldwin locomotive, planetarium — and home of the national Benjamin Franklin Memorial.
Neoclassical waterworks pavilions (1815–) on the Schuylkill below the Art Museum — a National Historic Landmark with a free interpretive center and the classic river-and-boathouse view.

rows.n: Edgar Allan Poe National Historic Site
rows.w: The only surviving Philadelphia home of Poe, with the cobwebbed cellar that may have inspired 'The Black Cat'; NPS-run, free.
Where the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the Constitution (1787) were debated and signed — a UNESCO World Heritage Site run by the National Park Service; free timed tickets.
Isaiah Zagar's labyrinthine folk-art environment of mirror, tile and bottle mosaics — half a block of it — on South Street.
Fifteen 19th-century rowing-club boathouses on the east bank of the Schuylkill, outlined in LED lights after dark — the city's postcard view from Kelly Drive.
John F. Kennedy Plaza, nicknamed for Robert Indiana's LOVE sculpture — one of Philly's most photographed spots, diagonal from City Hall. Free.
One of William Penn's five original squares, named for astronomer David Rittenhouse — the elegant heart of Center City for benches, people-watching and the Saturday farmers' market.
Penn's Landing's summer pop-up park — hammocks, floating barge gardens, a beer garden, food stalls and glowing lights over the Delaware (seasonal).

Opened for the 1976 Bicentennial as the first museum built by a major US city to preserve African American heritage; permanent exhibit 'Audacious Freedom: African Americans in Philadelphia 1776-1876' (Visit Philly).
One of William Penn's five original squares, revived 20 years ago with a carousel, Philly-landmark mini golf and the winter Chinese Lantern Festival (Visit Philly; Inquirer 2026).
One of the largest public Rodin collections outside Paris, fronted by bronze casts of The Thinker and The Gates of Hell; garden free.
Alexander Stirling Calder's 1924 fountain whose three Native American figures represent the Delaware, Schuylkill and Wissahickon — the centrepiece of Logan Circle.
Penn's southeast square, a Revolutionary-era burial ground now holding the Tomb of the Unknown Revolutionary War Soldier; part of Independence NHP.

rows.n: Cathedral Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul
rows.w: Pennsylvania's largest Catholic church (1864) and the only US cathedral in the Roman-Corinthian style, modelled on Rome's San Carlo al Corso, on Logan Square.

The largest municipal building in the US, crowned by Alexander Milne Calder's 37-ft William Penn; a 100-year-old elevator lifts four at a time to the glass-enclosed deck 548 ft up, the city's only 360° view.

rows.n: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts (PAFA)
rows.w: The nation's first art museum and school (1805), in Frank Furness's Victorian Gothic landmark fronted by Claes Oldenburg's 51-ft Paint Torch — American art from Peale to the present.
Mother church of the first Black denomination in the US (founded 1787 by Richard Allen) on the oldest parcel continuously owned by African Americans; the basement museum holds Allen's tomb.

National Historic Landmark department-store palace whose Grand Court houses the Wanamaker Organ, the world's largest operating musical instrument (28,750 pipes); after Macy's closed in 2025 the new owners brought back performances and the Christmas Light Show (Inquirer, Philly Mag 2025).
One of William Penn's five original squares, revived 20 years ago with a carousel, Philly-landmark mini golf and the winter Chinese Lantern Festival (Visit Philly; Inquirer 2026).
Benjamin Franklin's grave — visitors toss pennies on it for luck — among five signers of the Declaration buried here.
The 1873 Norman-cathedral-style headquarters of Pennsylvania's Freemasons across from City Hall, with seven lavish lodge halls in Egyptian, Moorish, Gothic and other styles; public tours.

rows.w: Reconstruction of the boarding house at 7th & Market where Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776 — part of Independence National Historical Park (NPS).
Dolley Madison's home with her first husband John Todd Jr. before his 1793 death — a restored middle-class Quaker house in Independence NHP (NPS).
